claims.text: A pre-oxidation heat treatment can induce controlled elemental segregation in a fixed-composition multiprincipal-element alloy.
Increasing elemental segregation enhances oxidation resistance relative to a homogenized condition.
The initial material is an unoxidized, homogenized CoCrFeNiMn-type multiprincipal-element alloy with minimal segregation.
The controlled oxidation comparison will be conducted cyclically in ambient air between approximately 800 and 1100 °C.
The degree and spatial distribution of segregation can be quantified using APT or TEM.
Elemental segregation modifies diffusion pathways and diffusion kinetics during oxidation.
Segregation alters local elemental concentrations and thereby affects oxide nucleation and selective oxidation.
Segregation promotes formation of a uniform, continuous, and adherent protective oxide scale.
The protective scale may contain mixed spinels or chromia/alumina phases.
Induced segregation suppresses formation of non-protective porous oxides.
Segregated specimens will exhibit lower oxidation weight gain than the untreated homogenized baseline.
Segregated specimens will form more uniform and adherent oxide scales than the baseline.
Segregated specimens will retain greater material integrity during cyclic high-temperature oxidation.
The predicted beneficial segregation effect should persist during cyclic oxidation up to roughly 1100 °C.
Excessive segregation or phase separation may produce unwanted oxide phases rather than protection.
A controlled comparison uses compositionally identical specimens differing only in segregation-inducing heat treatment.
Failure of segregated specimens to show improved oxidation resistance, or observation of degradation correlated with segregation, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: CoCrFeNiMn is given as the representative alloy, but alumina is proposed as a possible protective phase even though the stated composition contains no Al. Alumina would require a different Al-containing alloy within the loosely defined 'similar alloy' alternative.
